name: normalizer
intent: Convert semantically equivalent messages that arrive in different source formats into one canonical form at an integration seam, so every downstream consumer is written against exactly one message shape and format knowledge stays confined to per-format translators.
problem: Several producers send the same business message in different layouts - different field names, containers, units, currencies, date formats and encodings - and the shared downstream logic would otherwise have to branch on the source: every new partner, version or legacy system multiplies the conditional handling, and the semantic decisions about what a field really means get scattered across consumers.
context: Message-based integration at a boundary: an inbound stage receives messages from multiple partners, versions or legacy systems whose formats are not under your control, where the business meaning overlaps but the syntax does not, and where more than one consumer must interpret the data. Detection can rely on a type specifier carried by the transport, or - when the source is schema-less (CSV, XML without a schema, fixed-width files) - on documented heuristics such as the root element name, a schema probe, the field count or the file name.
benefits: Consumers are written once against the canonical message: no branching on the source system and no per-partner duplicates of the same business rule.
Adding a producer means adding one translator plus one routing entry, without touching downstream code - the seam stays closed for modification.
Source quirks (date layout, units, currency, field naming, encoding, optionality) live next to the mapping that documents them instead of being rediscovered by every consumer.
Validation, enrichment order and canonical-model evolution get a single home, which also makes the seam the natural place for contract tests and golden samples per format.
Format knowledge becomes an explicit, testable artifact: a partner's raw message can be replayed against its translator when the format changes.
Observability and replay see one shape to log, trace and re-publish, and there is an explicit place to attach provenance (source system and format version).
tradeoffs: The canonical model is a second permanent contract: every change ripples through all translators and all consumers, and it drifts into the union of every producer's concerns unless someone owns it.

Detection without a type specifier is heuristic - root element name, XPath probe, field count, file name or datatype channel - so ambiguous or overlapping formats misroute, and the wrong translator then produces a well-formed but semantically wrong canonical message.
Cost grows linearly with the number of sources: each format needs its own mapping, golden samples and regression suite, and retired formats still need removing from the routing table.
Translation is lossy by default: fields with no canonical counterpart, precision, scale, time zones and code lists are dropped or coerced unless an extension slot is designed in deliberately.
Every message pays an extra parse-map-serialize pass in the hot path, which is measurable work and extra copying at high volume compared with letting consumers read the wire format directly.
Provenance disappears after normalization: once the message is canonical, 'which partner sent which format version?' can only be answered if the normalizer deliberately retained it.

Parsing hostile input is concentrated at one seam, widening the attack surface of the parsers involved (tag-driven deserialization, pathological XML or CSV) even though it is also the single best place to validate and bound the input.

participants.responsibility: Composite inbound stage: accepts every supported source format, drives detection, translation, validation and publication, and owns the order of those steps.
Determines which format arrived - from a type specifier if the message carries one, otherwise from documented heuristics - and selects exactly one translator; it knows tags, never business semantics.

Performs the complete mapping of one source layout into the canonical message, including field renames, units, currency, dates, code lists and precision, and reports unmappable input instead of defaulting it.
The single application-independent shape every consumer depends on; it must not mirror any one producer and needs an owner and a version.
Merges correlated fragments of one logical message into the canonical message before publication, when a source delivers the message in parts.

Receives messages that cannot be detected, translated or validated, together with the original payload, so an unknown partner format never blocks the inbound flow and becomes the next regression sample.
Any downstream component that reads only the canonical message and contains no format-specific logic.

use_cases: B2B/EDI ingest: hundreds of partners deliver the same order or usage record as CSV, fixed-width, spreadsheet export or schema-less XML; the normalizer turns all of them into one canonical document before rating, billing or ledger posting.
Legacy and modern coexistence: SOAP/XML partners plus a JSON REST partner feed one domain event, normalized inside an anti-corruption layer so the domain model never grows three dialects.
Telemetry and log ingest: syslog, vendor JSON and CSV exports from appliances are normalized into one event schema before indexing, alerting or retention.
Configuration loading: environment variables, INI/TOML/YAML files, CLI flags and a database row are normalized into one settings object before validation and start-up decisions.
Broker and transport portability: messages from Kafka, SQS and AMQP envelopes are normalized into one internal envelope type so consumers do not depend on the transport's wire shape.
Data import and migration: several historical export versions (v1/v2/v3 dumps) are normalized to the current schema so the import logic exists once, not once per version.
Apache Camel's Normalizer EIP combines a Content-Based Router with per-format Message Translators (for example, employee and customer XML) so downstream routes receive one common person message.

MuleSoft Mule runtime's Transform Message/DataWeave component maps metadata-described XML, CSV, fixed-width, JSON and other payloads into one output structure before the rest of a flow applies business logic.

Amazon EventBridge Pipes input transformers reshape source or enrichment payloads with InputTemplate and JSONPath into the target contract, making the pipe edge a practical normalizer while reserved variables retain event provenance.
avoid_when: There is a single producer with a stable, versioned contract: one validating deserializer (or one Message Translator) is enough, and the router plus routing table are dead weight.
The formats differ in meaning, not only in syntax: forcing them into one canonical model merges distinct semantics - keep separate message types and let each consumer own its own.
You control the producers: standardize the wire format (Published Language) and delete the normalizer instead of maintaining it.
Audit or regulatory requirements need the original artifact verbatim: retain the raw payload and normalize only a projection rather than replacing the original with the canonical form.

Throughput-dominated bulk pipelines where the extra parse-map-serialize pass dominates: move the conversion upstream to the producer or into the stream processor once, instead of re-normalizing at every consumer.
anti_patterns: 'Normalization' as a switch statement repeated inside every consumer: the canonical form is never materialized, and each consumer re-learns all formats.
Trusting the sender's type specifier: routing on an unvalidated discriminator lets a caller choose the translator - and often the parser - that handles its payload.
Silent coercion as the error strategy: unmappable fields, unknown enum values and missing required data are defaulted away, producing a canonical message that looks valid and is wrong.
Canonical model as domain model: the normal-form DTO is promoted to the domain entity, so producer quirks (surrogate ids, split addresses, transport flags) leak into business rules.
One translator per producer version forever: version-specific mappings are copied instead of parameterized, and the routing table becomes a museum of dead formats.
Normalizing before the input is authenticated or bounded: a hostile payload gets translated with the same trusted path as a partner message.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: format knowledge (detector plus translators) is separated from semantics (canonical model and downstream rules).
Open/closed principle: new formats arrive through new translators and routing entries, not through edits to consumers.
Single responsibility: one translator per source format, one owner for the canonical model.
Dependency direction: translators depend on the canonical model, never the other way round, and consumers depend on nothing source-specific.
Fail fast at the boundary: an unknown or untranslatable format is a first-class error path, not a default branch.
Information hiding: consumers never see the raw format, translators never see the business rules.
best_practices: Give every message an explicit type specifier wherever you control a producer; treat heuristics as a documented fallback and pin their order and precedence.
Validate the canonical message against a versioned schema after translation with an explicit unknown-field policy (reject, retain or quarantine) instead of letting defaults mask missing data.
Keep a golden sample per source format and run every translator as a regression suite on each canonical-model change; store the sample together with the format version it represents.

Route neither silently nor fatally: unknown or untranslatable messages go to an invalid-message channel with the original payload, so the pipeline keeps flowing and the sample becomes the next test case.
Carry provenance (source system, format version, translator version) as canonical metadata for observability, replay and incident triage.
Normalize units, currency, time zone and code lists explicitly, document every lossy field, and never infer semantics from a field name alone.
Keep the canonical model independent of both the producers and the internal domain model, and map it into the domain at the inside edge.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Normalizer (Message Transformation chapter): route each message type through a custom Message Translator so that the resulting messages match a common format.
